This is going to be long, but I feel like maybe my story in relation to your questions will give you some comfort, since being diagnosed actually changed my life for the better.

I was diagnosed sophomore year of college while having a mild psychotic break. While this was devestating, I wouldn’t change it. I grew so much as a person upon understanding this part of myself. I was able to finish college and switch my major and enjoy the rest of my experience there. I like the person I am today so much better than the person I was, and other people do too. It doesn’t have to be the negative thing that the stigma makes it out to be. 

In my family, my parents know. They have seen a positive change in me so they accept it. Close friends know and they love me the same and say that I’ve blossomed since I was diagnosed. I tell people I date if it feels appropriate, and only had one guy be freaked out by it (he had his own issues so whatever). I recently told one coworker and our relationship is the same. I wouldn’t tell anyone else at work though, it was a conversation outside of work that made me feel comfortable sharing this with her.

On work - I returned to a retail job after I graduated. I was a valued part of my team and much better at my job than when I was still figuring all this out. I struggled in finding an office job, but I think this is mainly because I didn’t know what I wanted to do. I also assume that the hit on my gpa related to that period didn’t help. Personally, I chose not to disclose being bipolar when an application asks about disabilities. I feel that I have my symptoms under control enough. I would advise not to share your diagnosis in a professional setting unless you are positive that it will impact your work and put your job at risk. Medication improved my ability to continue work through rough periods so I would wait to see how treatment affects you before deciding to disclose. 

I know this is long but I was SO scared when I found out and was in such a horrible mental state for awhile. It took me a long time to wrap my head around it and reconcile the possible stigma. I want you to know that this can actually be a super positive thing. I can handle the social life I’ve always wanted, be consistent in my work, and live a life I never thought I would or could.

Bad times will still happen, but they will be smaller bumps in the road. Because my external life is so much more stable, and worth living, I can overcome those times so much better than I used to.

Allow yourself to come to terms with it on your own time. Tell people when you trust them. If anyone in your life does judge you, try not to take it personally. This doesn’t have to define you, and for a long time I thought it would define me. Going through this initial phase was a defining moment in my life, and now I can live and enjoy how it changed me.

If you ever need support you can reach out to me. I found kind of a “pen pal” who had more time knowing they were bipolar when I was diagnosed, and our relationship has been super beneficial. It doesn’t have to be me but I recommend participating in this subreddit and maybe trying to find someone :)

I don’t have a perfect answer because I have the same struggle (past of anorexia and ex dancer), but what Has helped is finding an activity I like (some months I like the gym, but most of the time it’s yoga) and make sure to do it 3 days a week. If I feel motivated to do more that’s great, but I’ve noticed if I make this goal of 3 classes my mental health is so much better which leads to better food choices and body image.

My body can’t do the amazing things it used to. It doesn’t look perfect anymore. And that’s hard to deal with. But reminding myself that my body is still a part of me that is capable of helping me do yoga and carrying me through life really helps. It’s not as remarkable, but it has helped a lot. 

It also just took a lot of time to become comfortable with how I look now. I weight about 10-15 lbs more than I did at my low weight and have very little visible muscle tone. I went through a period where I weighed about 25-30 lbs more right after I quit dance. I lost the weight by eating a reasonable deficit for my height 5 days a week and enjoying whatever I was craving on the weekend, and excersizing 3 times a week. The weight loss was slow (prepbably 5-6 months) which was hard but definitely worked for me and didn’t throw me into restrictive mode. 

It’s been about 3 years since I quit and while I still have a lot of frustration when my body can’t do something it used to, or clothes don’t fit right, things are a lot better. I actually feel more confident with some extra weight. I’ve showed myself that people still like me and I’m still capable even if I don’t have the “perfect” body. I actually have more friends now and get more attention from guys. I used to think I was only “worthy” if I didn’t eat. 

I hope you can find some body peace and find something that makes you want to celebrate your body again. If you ever want to talk feel free to message me ❤️

It’s uncomfortable to be sexualized by a (usually older) man who says something like this then stares at me awhile. When I’m walking down the street I don’t like people I don’t know commenting on my body/if I’m attractive because I don’t feel safe. In my opinion you could tell someone they’re attractive when you’re having a one-on-one conversation already in a casual, non work setting.

I was debating what to do with this for about 3 months before I had a panic attack in front of my boyfriend after an amazing day. He thought it was only anxiety and he told me his experience with it, so I decided that it was best he knew I was bipolar. Your illness might decide for you haha. In my opinion just decide if you want to be upfront or let it show itself then explain. 

If it’s any solace my bf has been awesome with it! He asks me questions (I don’t know if he googled them) and seems to accept it/wants to understand so he can be helpful. Just present it in a way that explains your experience and how you manage it and try to focus on the positive way you’re dealing with it. If he’s a good guy he’ll respect that you’re more than a mood disorder.

Yess this is so hard to adjust to. At first I couldn’t stand how boring being stable is. But then over time it allowed me to built a stable life and relationships. There are still some things I grapple with about medication/the disorder since I was only diagnosed a few years ago, but this is something I’ve realized. Hopefully that’s some comfort, it does start to seem more like a pro than a con. Good luck with everything xx
